performers: Enrico Caruso, tenor; Salvatore Cottone, piano
question: How does the tenor shape the aria above piano accompaniment?
intro: Caruso sings with Salvatore Cottone at the piano on this ten-inch Gramophone master, recorded in Milan in 1902. The short side is not interchangeable with the longer orchestral recording of 1907: compare only their shared aria passage.

sections.label: Central expansion
sections.mNote: analysis landmark, not an aligned word or score bar

sections.label: Later crest
sections.mNote: a stronger recorded span precedes the final withdrawal

cues.title: Tenor and piano
cues.text: Caruso sings in Italian with Salvatore Cottone at the piano. Follow the voice across the piano’s separate attacks; the accompaniment is not the orchestral texture heard in his 1907 remake.
cues.evidence: DAHR Gramophone 2875b identifies Caruso, Cottone, Italian text and piano accompaniment: https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/refer/1000003400. No exact vocal entrance is claimed.

cues.title: A performance inside the opera
cues.text: Canio must prepare to play a clown after discovering his wife’s infidelity. The aria closes Act I of Pagliacci: its commands to perform belong to that dramatic situation, not to a recording-session anecdote.
cues.evidence: The dramatic situation and 1892 opera are documented at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vesti_la_giubba. No individual sung word is assigned to this timestamp.

cues.title: A central recorded rise
cues.text: The central passage grows into a stronger recorded span after an earlier relaxation. Follow the entire phrase across the change, without taking the surface noise as a guide to the singer’s articulation.
cues.evidence: The report shows −24.6 dB at 0:35 and −11.8 dB at 0:50, with a boundary at 0:46. Noise-contaminated onset counts do not establish syllables or breath points.

cues.title: The later crest
cues.text: The later phrase reaches the side’s strongest recorded stretch. Hear how the voice sustains its direction across successive rises rather than expecting one isolated climactic attack.
cues.evidence: Boundary at 1:18; the 1:20, 1:25, 1:30 and 1:35 windows are among the report’s five highest. This is relative level within the transfer, not vocal loudness measured against another record.

cues.title: Releasing the ending
cues.text: The final span loses weight before the remaining sound disappears. Continue through the release of the piano and voice, distinguishing that decay from the disc’s surface sound.
cues.evidence: The strongest boundary is at 1:40, followed by lower level; the report falls from −16.5 dB at 1:50 to −47.2 dB at 2:00. No exact final word or breath is located.

transitions.title: The phrase recovers recorded weight
transitions.how: The quieter opening span leads into a stronger phrase. Tenor and piano remain the same forces; the change is in the phrase’s weight, not a new instrumental entrance.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 0:46; relative level rises from the low 0:35 window to the high 0:50 window.

transitions.title: Another phrase reaches a larger crest
transitions.how: The continuing vocal line reaches the strongest late span. Listen across several successive gestures rather than turning the section marker into the instant of a particular word.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 1:18; the 1:20–1:35 windows dominate the report’s highest levels.

transitions.title: The late crest recedes
transitions.how: The late swell gives way to a less weighted closing span. The remaining voice and piano sound then diminish towards the surface noise at the end of the side.
transitions.evidence: Strongest boundary at 1:40; reduced level at 1:40–1:50 is followed by a sharp fall at 1:55–2:00.
